lessons.title: Tenses Revision
lessons.grammar_topic: 12 ZAMON — TAKROR (Simple / Continuous / Perfect / Perfect Continuous × Present / Past / Future)
lessons.book_ref: Student's book IELTS 3.0: Lesson 1 – Tenses revision (12 qatorli jadval); LEARNING (63 so'z); Reading — Ishoqxon Ibrat (Jony Academy matni); kitob Topic 1–5 uyga; Writing: Advantages and disadvantages of using public transport.
objectives: 12 zamon formulasini 3×4 jadvalda bir nafasda ayta olish.
Vaqt ko'rsatkichiga qarab zamonni tanlash (every day / now / yesterday / by 2030 / for two years…).
Bitta vaziyatni 4 zamon bilan ifodalash (I study / am studying / have studied / have been studying).
Ta'lim CORE 20 lug'ati bilan o'z o'qish uslubi haqida gapirish; Writing 1: advantages/disadvantages tuzilmasi.
timeline: Ustoz bitta fe'l aytadi: "learn". O'quvchilar aylanib 12 zamonda gap tuzadi: I learn / I learned / I will learn / I am learning… Kim to'xtab qolsa — keyingisi davom etadi.
20 savol, 15 soniya; oldingi dars lug'ati + grammatikasi.

Kitob jadvali 12 qator: har zamon — formula — misol. Doskada 3×4 katak: qatorlar Present/Past/Future, ustunlar Simple/Continuous/Perfect/Perfect Continuous. O'quvchilar kataklarni o'zlari to'ldiradi, keyin kitob bilan solishtiradi.
Har so'z bilan yangi grammatika qolipida gap.
Kitob: formula → gap → tarjima; warm-up / normativ / coin me'yorlari.
Sinf matni + 3 topshiriq; kitob Topic'lari uyga.
Yangi grammatika bilan 5 gap (yozma) yoki 1 daqiqa og'zaki.
Ko'p uchragan xatolar doskada; STRONG lug'at kuchlilarga.

intro: SIMPLE — fakt, odat, tugagan ish: reads / drove / will study.
CONTINUOUS — jarayon shu paytda: am learning / were sleeping / will be travelling.
PERFECT — nuqtagacha tugagan, natija: has read / had finished / will have finished.
PERFECT CONTINUOUS — nuqtagacha davom etgan jarayon: have been learning / had been sleeping / will have been waiting.
Qoida: Present — hozir; Past — o'tgan nuqta; Future — kelajak nuqta. Ustun ma'noni, qator vaqtni beradi.
formulas: He reads a book every day. / I am learning English.
U har kuni kitob o'qiydi. / Men ingliz tili o'rganyapman.
She drove a car yesterday. / We were sleeping.
U kecha mashina haydadi. / Biz uxlayotgan edik.
S + will + V1 / S + will be + V-ing
We will study hard next week. / We will be travelling around the world.
Kelasi hafta qattiq o'qiymiz. / Biz dunyo bo'ylab sayohat qilayotgan bo'lamiz.
S + have/has + V3 / S + have/has been + V-ing
He has read 10 books so far. / I have been learning English for 2 years.
U hozirgacha 10 kitob o'qidi. / Men 2 yildan beri ingliz tili o'rganyapman.
S + had + V3 / S + had been + V-ing
He had finished elementary level by 2020. / He had been sleeping for 2 hours by the time he arrived.
U 2020-gacha boshlang'ich darajani tugatgan edi. / U kelguncha 2 soat uxlayotgan edi.
S + will have + V3 / S + will have been + V-ing
We will have finished university by 2030. / I will have been waiting for 2 hours by noon.
2030-gacha universitetni tugatib bo'lamiz. / Tushgacha 2 soat kutayotgan bo'laman.
presentation: How do you usually learn new words?
I usually write them down and review them every evening.
What are you learning right now?
I'm revising the twelve tenses.
What did you learn yesterday?

What were you doing at 8 pm last night?
I was doing my homework.

How long have you been studying English?

Will you be studying at 9 tomorrow?
Yes, I'll be studying in the library.

By 2030, how long will you have been learning English?
I will have been learning it for eight years.
notes: Vaqt ko'rsatkichlari: every day/usually → Present Simple; now/at the moment → Present Continuous; yesterday/ago/in 2020 → Past Simple; while/at 8 pm → Past Continuous; so far/already/yet/since/for → Present Perfect (Continuous); by the time + Past → Past Perfect; by 2030 → Future Perfect.
Holat fe'llari (know, believe, own, belong) continuous'da ishlatilmaydi.

Writing 1 tuzilmasi (advantages/disadvantages): kirish (1–2 gap) → afzalliklar (2 ta, misol bilan) → kamchiliklar (2 ta) → xulosa (o'z fikri). 150+ so'z. Bog'lovchilar: firstly, in addition, however, on the other hand, in conclusion.
Learning lug'ati ikki qatlam: akademik otlar (retention, curriculum) + phrasal verbs (look up, brush up on, catch up on).
mistakes: She has studied here since two years.
She has studied here for two years.
By the time I arrived, the lesson started.
I will learn 500 words by June. (tugallik)
I will have learned 500 words by June.
He is reading books every day.

how: CORE 20 — ta'lim jarayonining asosiy otlari va iboralari; STRONG — o'rganish strategiyalari; SUPER — phrasal verbs (look up, figure out, brush up on…).
Har so'zga o'quvchi o'zi tanlagan zamonda gap tuzadi va zamonni aytadi: "I have been brushing up on my grammar — Present Perfect Continuous."

reading.title: Ishaqkhan Ibrat — the man who taught himself six languages
text: Ishaqkhan Ibrat was born in 1862 in To'raqo'rg'on, near Namangan. His mother was a teacher, and by the age of ten he had already learned to read and write in three alphabets. He studied at a madrasa in Kokand, but the old system disappointed him: students memorized texts for years without understanding them. "Learning without comprehension is like carrying water in a basket," he wrote later.

In the 1890s Ibrat travelled to Istanbul, Cairo, Jeddah and India. While he was travelling, he was learning: by the time he returned, he had taught himself Arabic, Persian, Turkish, Hindi and Russian, and he had been studying English for two years. He wrote the first six-language dictionary in Turkestan.

When he came home, he opened a new-method school where children learned by understanding, not by memorization. He bought a printing press in 1908 — the first in the region — and printed textbooks himself. He also built a library that anyone could use. Many of his ideas — active learning, critical thinking, self-directed study — are exactly what modern schools are trying to do today.
Ibrat died in 1937. His house in To'raqo'rg'on is now a museum, and thousands of students visit it every year. If he were alive, he would probably be running an online school.

lessons.title: Used to / Be used to
lessons.grammar_topic: USED TO + V1 (o'tgan odat) vs BE/GET USED TO + V-ing (o'rganib qolgan)
lessons.book_ref: Student's book IELTS 3.0: Lesson 2 – Used to / to be used to (ikki jadval); TECHNOLOGY (54 so'z); Reading — Steve Jobs (Jony Academy matni); kitob Topic 6–10 uyga.
objectives: used to + V1 bilan o'tgan odatlarni tasdiq, inkor va savolda aytish.
be used to + V-ing/ot bilan hozirgi o'rganib qolgan holatni aytish; get used to — jarayon.
Ikki qolipni chalkashtirmaslik: used to (o'tgan) — be used to (hozir), V1 — V-ing.
Texnologiya CORE 20 bilan o'zgarishlar haqida gapirish (people used to…, now we are used to…).
timeline: Ustoz eski telefon rasmini ko'rsatadi: "People used to send SMS. Now we are used to sending voice messages." Savol: "What did you use to do that you don't do now?"
20 savol, 15 soniya; oldingi dars lug'ati + grammatikasi.

Kitob jadvallari: USED TO + V1 (o'tmishda bo'lgan, hozir yo'q odat): I used to smoke / didn't use to / Did you use to…?; BE USED TO + V-ing (o'rganib qolgan holat): I am used to smoking / I'm not used to / Are you used to…? Qo'shimcha: GET USED TO + V-ing (o'rganib bormoq).
Har so'z bilan yangi grammatika qolipida gap.
Kitob: formula → gap → tarjima; warm-up / normativ / coin me'yorlari.
Sinf matni + 3 topshiriq; kitob Topic'lari uyga.
Yangi grammatika bilan 5 gap (yozma) yoki 1 daqiqa og'zaki.
Ko'p uchragan xatolar doskada; STRONG lug'at kuchlilarga.

intro: USED TO + V1 — oldin bo'lgan, hozir yo'q odat/holat: "I used to smoke" (hozir chekmayman). Inkor: didn't use to; savol: Did you use to…?
BE USED TO + V-ing / ot — o'rganib qolgan, odatiy: "I am used to smoking" (menga odatiy). Inkor: am not used to; savol: Are you used to…?
GET USED TO + V-ing — o'rganib bormoq (jarayon): "I'm getting used to online lessons."
Farq: used to → o'tgan zamon, V1; be/get used to → hozir, V-ing (to — predlog!).
formulas: I didn't use to drink coffee.
I am used to smoking. / I'm used to the noise.
Men chekishga o'rganib qolganman. / Shovqinga o'rganganman.
S + be + not + used to + V-ing / Be + S + used to + V-ing?
I'm not used to drinking coffee. / Are you used to working online?
Qahva ichishga o'rganmaganman. / Onlayn ishlashga o'rganganmisan?
S + get/is getting + used to + V-ing
I'm getting used to the new app.
presentation: Did you use to have a phone at 10?
No, I didn't use to have one. I got my first phone at 13.
What did people use to do before the internet?
They used to write letters and read newspapers.
Are you used to studying online?
Yes, I'm used to it now — we did it for two years.
Did your parents use to play computer games?
No, they didn't use to. There were no computers.
Are you getting used to the new version of the app?
Slowly. I'm still not used to the new interface.
Did your grandfather use to watch TV?
He used to listen to the radio.
Are you used to typing fast?
Yes, I'm used to typing without looking.
What did you use to be afraid of?

Is your grandmother used to smartphones?
She's getting used to video calls with us.
Did people use to think the internet was dangerous?
Yes, many people used to think so.
notes: used to — faqat o'tgan zamon; hozirgi odat uchun Present Simple + usually.
"used to" holat uchun ham: I used to be shy / There used to be a shop here.
be used to + ot ham bo'ladi: I'm used to the cold. get used to + V-ing: It takes time to get used to living abroad.
Texnologiya lug'ati: innovation, digitalization, AI, IoT, AR/VR, cutting-edge, user-friendly; phrasal: come up with, carry out, scale up, log in.
mistakes: I am used to play games.
I am used to playing games.
I used to smoke. / I am used to smoking.
People are used to send letters before.
People used to send letters before.

how: CORE 20 — zamonaviy texnologiya otlari (innovation, AI, smart devices…); STRONG — kuchli sifat-birikmalar (cutting-edge, user-friendly); SUPER — phrasal verbs va sohaviy iboralar.
Har so'zga juft gap: "People used to … / Now we are used to …" — texnologiya o'zgarishi.

reading.title: Steve Jobs — phones used to have buttons
text: Steve Jobs was born in 1955 in San Francisco and was adopted as a baby. He used to be a difficult student: he didn't use to do his homework, and he dropped out of college after six months. But he used to sit in on classes that interested him — one of them was calligraphy, and years later that class gave the Mac its beautiful fonts.

In 1976 Jobs and his friend Steve Wozniak started Apple in a garage. Computers used to be huge machines for companies; the two Steves came up with a computer for ordinary people. Apple grew fast, but in 1985 Jobs was fired from his own company. "It was the best thing that could have happened to me," he said later.

He came back in 1997, when Apple was almost bankrupt. In the next ten years he brought about three revolutions: the iPod (2001), the iPhone (2007) and the iPad (2010). Before the iPhone, phones used to have small buttons and tiny screens; people weren't used to touching a screen. Today we are so used to it that children try to touch the TV.

Jobs died in 2011. His advice to students is still quoted everywhere: "Stay hungry, stay foolish." Uzbek startups at IT Park often say they are trying to do what Apple used to do in a garage — build something people don't know they need yet.

intro: Tag = yordamchi fe'l + olmosh: "He is a teacher, isn't he?" "They went home, didn't they?"
Tasdiq gap → inkor tag; inkor gap → tasdiq tag.
Yordamchi fe'l gapdagi bilan bir xil: be → be; Present Simple → do/does; Past Simple → did; will; modals (can, must, should).
Maxsus: I am → aren't I?; Let's → shall we?; buyruq → will you?; nobody/nothing/never (inkor ma'no) → tasdiq tag; there is → isn't there?

reading.title: Alisher Usmanov — he started with nothing, didn't he?
text: Alisher Usmanov was born in 1953 in Chust, a small town in Namangan region. He didn't come from a business family, did he? No — his father was a prosecutor. As a teenager Alisher was a fencer: he won championships in Uzbekistan and dreamed of the Olympics. He was tall and strong, wasn't he? Yes — 1.90 m and the best sabre fencer in the republic.

In the 1980s his life changed twice. First he spent six years in prison, and later the court said he had been innocent. Then, in the 1990s, he started his first businesses: he used to trade in plastic bags and cigarettes, and he set up a company that made packaging. He took calculated risks, didn't he? He did: he bought shares in steel and mining companies that nobody wanted, and in the 2000s they became worth billions.

Usmanov was also an early investor in technology. He raised capital for Facebook in 2009, when many people thought social media was a bubble, and he bought a share of Alibaba before it became a giant. "You have to think outside the box, don't you?" he once said. He also owned part of Arsenal football club for eleven years.

Today Usmanov is known in Uzbekistan mostly for charity: he has built schools, mosques and hospitals in Namangan and Tashkent, and he has paid for the restoration of historic buildings. He is still the president of the International Fencing Federation — sport didn't leave him, did it?

reading.title: Al-Farabi — the Second Teacher who classified everything
text: Abu Nasr al-Farabi was born around 870 in Farab (Otrar), on the Syr Darya, in a Turkic family. Nobody knows much about his childhood, but everyone agrees on one thing: he was one of the greatest minds of the Islamic Golden Age. In the Muslim world he is called "the Second Teacher" — the first was Aristotle.

Farabi studied in Bukhara and Samarkand, and then travelled to Baghdad, where anyone with talent could find teachers and books. He learned Greek and wrote commentaries on Aristotle that were so clear that Ibn Sina said: "I read Aristotle's Metaphysics forty times and understood nothing; then I found Farabi's commentary, and everything became clear."

Farabi believed that nothing in science works without logic. He wrote "The Classification of the Sciences", a book that organised everything that was known at the time: mathematics, physics, medicine, music and language. He also wrote about the ideal city, where everyone works together and nobody is ignored — one of the first books about how a good society should be built.

He was also a musician: he wrote "The Great Book of Music", and some say he invented a musical instrument. Farabi died in Damascus in 950. Today his name is on universities in Almaty and Tashkent, and every philosopher still reads him.

Kitob jadvali 7 qator: must have (ishonchli taxmin), may/might have (ehtimol), can't/couldn't have (bo'lishi mumkin emas), should/ought to have (kerak edi — afsus), shouldn't have (qilmasligi kerak edi — tanbeh), could have (qila olardi, lekin qilmadi), needn't have (shart emas edi, lekin qilindi). intro: TAXMIN (o'tgan): must have + V3 — 90% ishonch ("He must have left early"); may/might have — 50% ("She might have forgotten"); can't/couldn't have — 0% ("They can't have seen us").

BAHO (o'tgan): should have — kerak edi, qilinmadi ("I should have studied more"); shouldn't have — qilmaslik kerak edi ("You shouldn't have lied"); could have — qila olardi ("She could have won"); needn't have — shart emas edi, lekin qildi ("You needn't have bought so much").
Shakl o'zgarmaydi: modal + have + V3 — hamma shaxs uchun; "should had", "must has" — xato.
formulas: She might have forgotten my message.
Ular bizni ko'rgan bo'lishi mumkin emas.

S + could have + V3 / S + needn't have + V3

U poygada yutishi mumkin edi. / Bunchalik ko'p ovqat olishing shart emas edi.

reading.title: Kamoliddin Behzod — the miniature master of Herat
text: Kamoliddin Behzod was born around 1455 in Herat, which was then the cultural capital of the Timurid state. His parents died when he was a child, and he must have been very talented, because the poet and minister Alisher Navoi took him into his care and sent him to the best workshop in the city.

Behzod became the greatest master of the Persian-Turkic miniature. His paintings are small — often the size of a page — but they can't have been painted quickly: in one picture you may see fifty people, each with a different face, different clothes and a different emotion. He must have used a brush with a single hair for the smallest details. Historians say he might have been the first artist in the East to paint real people, not ideal types: builders, cooks, beggars, a tired king.

In 1507 the Uzbek ruler Shaybani Khan took Herat, and later Behzod moved to Tabriz, where he directed the royal library. His students spread his style to Bukhara, India and Turkey. European art historians have called him "the Raphael of the East" — though he could never have seen a European painting.

Behzod died around 1535. Most of his works are now in museums in London, Cairo and Tehran; Uzbekistan should have kept more of them, people say, but in the 16th century nobody thought about museums. The National Institute of Arts in Tashkent is named after him.

Kitob jadvali 11 qator: very (juda), too (haddan tashqari + to-infinitive), enough (sifatdan KEYIN), so…that (natija), quite / rather / fairly (birmuncha), almost (deyarli), absolutely / completely / utterly (kuchli sifatlar bilan: absolutely amazing, completely empty, utterly disappointed).

intro: VERY — oddiy kuchaytirish: very tired. TOO — haddan tashqari, salbiy natija: too hot to go outside. ENOUGH — sifatdan keyin: warm enough to swim.
SO + adj + THAT + natija: He was so happy that he cried. (such + ot + that: such a good doctor that…)
QUITE / RATHER / FAIRLY — "birmuncha, ancha": quite interesting, rather cold, fairly well. ALMOST — deyarli: almost fell asleep.
Kuchli sifatlar (amazing, exhausted, freezing, furious) bilan very EMAS: absolutely amazing, completely empty, utterly disappointed.

reading.title: Oksana Chusovitina — the gymnast who is never too old
text: Oksana Chusovitina was born in 1975 in Bukhara. Gymnasts usually retire at 20, because the sport is so hard on the body that almost nobody can continue longer. Oksana has competed at eight Olympic Games — from Barcelona 1992 to Tokyo 2021 — and that is absolutely unique in the history of the sport.

Her first gold came in 1992, when she was only 17. Then she married, had a son, and kept training. In 2002 her son Alisher was diagnosed with leukaemia, a form of cancer. The treatment in Germany was far too expensive for the family, so Oksana made a decision: she would compete for money in every competition she could. "As long as I win, my son is fine," she said. She competed for Germany for several years, and Alisher recovered completely.

At the London Olympics in 2012 she was 37 — old enough to be the mother of the other gymnasts. In Tokyo, at 46, she was still fit enough to compete on the vault. Her secret is quite simple: a balanced diet, enough sleep, regular exercise and no junk food. "My body is very tired," she says, "but my head is not."

In 2021 she returned to Uzbekistan and now trains young gymnasts in Tashkent. She was so popular in Tokyo that the whole stadium stood up when she finished. Was it her last Olympics? "Maybe," she smiles. "But I said that in 2012 too."

YOZMA NORMATIV — Adverbs of degree lug'ati

Kitob jadvali 9 qator: HOWEVER / NEVERTHELESS / ON THE OTHER HAND / IN CONTRAST / CONVERSELY / STILL — yangi gap boshida, vergul bilan; WHEREAS / WHILE — ikki gapni bitta gapga bog'laydi (vergul); YET — "ammo" (and/but kabi, vergul bilan). Writing uchun eng muhim bo'lovchilar.
Har so'z bilan yangi grammatika qolipida gap.
Kitob: formula → gap → tarjima; warm-up / normativ / coin me'yorlari.
Sinf matni + 3 topshiriq; kitob Topic'lari uyga.
Yangi grammatika bilan 5 gap (yozma) yoki 1 daqiqa og'zaki.
Ko'p uchragan xatolar doskada; STRONG lug'at kuchlilarga.

intro: HOWEVER / NEVERTHELESS / STILL — "biroq, shunga qaramay": yangi gap boshida, vergul: "The test was difficult. However, I passed it."
ON THE OTHER HAND / IN CONTRAST / CONVERSELY — ikki tomon/farq: "Living in a city is convenient. On the other hand, it can be noisy."
WHEREAS / WHILE — bitta gap ichida farq: "She enjoys classical music, whereas he prefers rock."
YET — "ammo" bog'lovchi: "She is smart, yet she often makes mistakes." (but dan kuchliroq, rasmiy).
formulas: The test was difficult. However, I passed it.
Test qiyin edi. Biroq men undan o'tdim.
Gap 1. Nevertheless, gap 2. / Gap 1. Still, gap 2.
He was tired. Nevertheless, he continued working. / It was raining. Still, they went for a walk.
U charchagan edi. Shunga qaramay, ishlashda davom etdi. / Yomg'ir yog'ayotgan edi. Shunga qaramay, sayrga chiqishdi.
Gap 1. On the other hand, gap 2.
Living in a city is convenient. On the other hand, it can be noisy.
Shaharda yashash qulay. Boshqa tomondan, shovqinli bo'lishi mumkin.
She is very shy. In contrast, her brother is outgoing.
U juda tortinchoq. Aksincha, ukasi kirishimli.
She enjoys classical music, whereas he prefers rock. / Some people like coffee, while others prefer tea.
U klassik musiqani yoqtiradi, holbuki u rokni afzal ko'radi. / Ba'zilar qahvani yoqtiradi, boshqalar esa choyni.
She is smart, yet she often makes mistakes.
U aqlli, ammo tez-tez xato qiladi.

reading.title: Babur — the king who lost everything, yet wrote it all down
text: Zahiriddin Muhammad Babur was born in 1483 in Andijan. He became the ruler of Fergana at 12, when his father died. However, his uncles and neighbours wanted his land, and by the age of 20 he had lost Fergana, won Samarkand twice and lost it twice. Most princes in his position gave up. Babur, nevertheless, kept moving.

In 1504 he crossed the mountains with a few hundred men and took Kabul. It was a small, poor city, whereas Samarkand had been the jewel of Asia. Still, Kabul became his home for twenty years. He planted gardens, wrote poems and studied the land. Then, in 1526, he led an expedition to India and defeated a much larger army at Panipat. He became the first Mughal emperor; his descendants ruled India for more than 300 years.

Babur is famous today mainly for one thing: his memoir, the "Baburnama". Kings usually praised themselves. In contrast, Babur wrote about his mistakes, his fears and his homesickness with complete honesty. He described every city, fruit, animal and river he saw — the book is a travel guide to Central Asia and India in the 16th century. He wrote it in Chagatai Turkic, the language of Navoi, yet it has been translated into more than 30 languages.

He died in Agra in 1530, only four years after his victory. He was rich and powerful. On the other hand, he was homesick to the end: "The melons of Fergana," he wrote, "I have never tasted anything like them."

YOZMA NORMATIV — Adverbs of contrast lug'ati

Kitob jadvali 7 qator: here / there / everywhere / somewhere / anywhere / nowhere / nearby — fe'ldan keyin (Verb + adverb). Qo'shimcha: abroad, upstairs/downstairs, indoors/outdoors, inside/outside, away, back, home (predlogsiz: go home, live abroad). intro: HERE / THERE — shu yerda / u yerda: "She is here now." "He is there waiting."
EVERYWHERE — hamma joyda; SOMEWHERE — qayerdadir (tasdiq); ANYWHERE — biror joyda (savol/inkor); NOWHERE — hech qayerda (inkor ma'no, fe'l tasdiq).
NEARBY — yaqinda: "There is a bank nearby." Qo'shimcha: abroad, upstairs, downstairs, indoors, outdoors, inside, outside, away, back, home, downtown, far away.
O'rin: fe'ldan keyin (go there), ob'ektdan keyin (put it here), odatda vaqt ravishidan oldin: "We went there yesterday."
formulas: She is here now. / He is there waiting for you.
U hozir shu yerda. / U u yerda seni kutyapti.
They looked everywhere, but they couldn't find the keys.
Ular hamma joydan qidirdi, lekin kalitlarni topa olmadi.

presentation: Where did the battle take place?

reading.title: Jaloliddin Manguberdi — the prince who had nowhere to go
text: Jaloliddin Manguberdi was born in 1199 in Khorezm, the son of the Khorezmshah Muhammad II. His father ruled over a huge empire that spread everywhere from the Caspian Sea to India. Then, in 1219, Genghis Khan invaded. City after city fell; Bukhara, Samarkand and Urgench were destroyed. The Shah fled somewhere to the west and died on a small island in the Caspian. His son did not flee.

Jaloliddin gathered soldiers wherever he could and fought the Mongols here and there for eleven years. His most famous battle took place in 1221 on the banks of the Indus river, in today's Pakistan. His army was surrounded; there was nowhere to retreat. Jaloliddin rode his horse off a cliff into the river and swam across with his weapons. Genghis Khan, watching from the bank, said to his sons: "A father should have a son like this."

He carried on fighting abroad — in India, Iran, Georgia and Iraq — always looking for allies, but he found none anywhere. In 1231 he was killed in the mountains of Kurdistan. Nobody knows where his grave is.

For 700 years his story lived only in chronicles. Today his monument stands in Urgench, his name is on an order of the Republic of Uzbekistan, and every schoolchild knows him as the man who never surrendered.

20 savol, 15 soniya; oldingi dars lug'ati + grammatikasi.
YOZMA NORMATIV — Adverbs of place lug'ati

Kitob jadvali 8 qator: LIKE + ot (o'xshash: like a professional); AS + ot (sifatida: as a teacher); AS IF / AS THOUGH + gap (xuddi …dek; Past Simple — real emas: as if he knew everything); SUCH AS + misollar; THE SAME AS; JUST AS; UNLIKE + ot (farqli o'laroq); INSTEAD OF + ot/V-ing (o'rniga).

intro: LIKE + ot/olmosh — "kabi, o'xshab": She dances like a professional. (u professional emas).
AS + ot — "sifatida" (haqiqiy vazifa): She works as a teacher. (u o'qituvchi).
AS IF / AS THOUGH + gap — "xuddi …dek": real: He looks as if he is tired; noreal: He talks as if he knew everything (bilmaydi) / as if he were a king.
SUCH AS — misollar: fruits such as apples. THE SAME AS — bir xil. JUST AS — xuddi … kabi (gap). UNLIKE — farqli o'laroq. INSTEAD OF — o'rniga (+ ot / V-ing).
formulas: S + V + as if + gap (Past Simple — noreal)

Olma va banan kabi mevalarni yaxshi ko'raman.
the same as + ot; just as + gap/ot
This jacket is the same as mine. / She sings just as her mother did.
Bu kurtka meniki bilan bir xil. / U xuddi onasi kuylagandek kuylaydi.
Unlike his brother, he is very shy. / I'll have tea instead of coffee.
Akasidan farqli o'laroq, u juda tortinchoq. / Qahva o'rniga choy ichaman.

reading.title: Usain Bolt — born to run, or made to run?
text: Usain Bolt was born in 1986 in a small village in Jamaica. As a boy he played cricket and football, just as every Jamaican child does, and he ran like the wind — but he didn't like training. His coach said he behaved as if the world record would come by itself.

It didn't, but something else did: at the Beijing Olympics in 2008 Bolt ran 100 metres in 9.69 seconds, and in Berlin in 2009 he set a world record of 9.58 seconds that nobody has beaten. He won eight Olympic gold medals and became the most famous sprinter in history. Unlike most sprinters, who are short and compact, Bolt is 1.95 m tall.

Scientists have studied him like a laboratory experiment. Genetics is part of the answer: Bolt has a large number of fast-twitch muscle fibres, a trait that is inherited, and a gene variant called ACTN3 that most top sprinters share. Many people in Jamaica have this "speed gene", as if the whole island were selected for running. But genes are not everything. Bolt trained six hours a day, ate 100 chicken nuggets in Beijing (he says!) and worked with the same coach for fifteen years.

Was he born to run or made to run? Scientists answer: both. "Nature loads the gun," they say, "and nurture pulls the trigger." Bolt retired in 2017 and now works as a businessman and a father — and he still jokes that his children run as though they had his legs.

intro: Type 2: If + Past Simple, would + V1 — hozir/kelajak noreal. Type 3: If + Past Perfect, would have + V3 — o'tgan noreal.
MIXED 1 (o'tgan → hozir): "If I had studied harder (o'tgan), I would be successful now (hozir)."
MIXED 2 (hozir → o'tgan): "If he were more careful (doimiy xarakter), he wouldn't have made that mistake (o'tgan)."
Ko'rsatkichlar: now / today / still — hozirgi yarim; yesterday / last year / then — o'tgan yarim.
formulas: If + Past Perfect, S + would + V1 (now)

reading.title: Mark Zuckerberg — the ten-billion-dollar bet on virtual reality
text: Mark Zuckerberg was born in 1984 in New York. He wrote his first program at 12, and at Harvard, in 2004, he built a website for students in his dormitory. It was called "The Facebook". If he had stayed at Harvard, he would probably be a computer science professor now. Instead, he dropped out, moved to California and launched the site to the world. By 2012 it had a billion users.

In 2014 Zuckerberg made a decision that surprised everybody: he paid two billion dollars for Oculus, a small company that made VR headsets. "If we don't build the next platform," he said, "someone else will." Critics laughed. Headsets were heavy, the graphics were poor, and many users got motion sickness. If the technology had been ready, VR would be everywhere now. It wasn't.

In 2021 he went further: he renamed the whole company Meta and promised a "metaverse" — a shared virtual world where people would work, study and meet as avatars. The company has spent more than fifty billion dollars on it. If he weren't so sure about the future, he would have stopped years ago. Many investors wish he had.

Today Meta's headsets are the most popular in the world, and millions of students use them for simulations, virtual tours and games. Was the bet right? Nobody knows yet. If the metaverse becomes real, Zuckerberg will be remembered as a visionary. If it doesn't, people will say that if he had put that money into AI earlier, Meta would be far ahead now. Either way, he says, "the biggest risk is not taking any risk."

reading.title: Rustam Kasimdzhanov — the Uzbek who became world chess champion
text: Rustam Kasimdzhanov was born in 1979 in Tashkent. Every child in his neighbourhood played football; Rustam played chess. Each evening his father set up the board, and by the age of 12 the boy was beating every adult in the club. At 19 he became a grandmaster.

In 2004 the World Chess Championship was held in Tripoli, Libya, as a knockout tournament: 128 players, and after each round half of them went home. Nobody expected the underdog from Uzbekistan to survive the first week. But he beat every opponent, including former champions, and in the final he faced Michael Adams of England. Each of the six classical games was hard; neither player could get a clear lead, and the match went to tiebreaks. Kasimdzhanov won — and became FIDE World Champion, the first and only from Central Asia.

He never won the title again, but every top player knows his name: he has been the second (assistant) of Viswanathan Anand and Fabiano Caruana, helping them prepare openings for their world championship matches. "Either you work every day," he says, "or you lose. There is no third option."

Today he lives in Germany, plays for Uzbekistan and coaches young players. In 2022 the Uzbek team, with an average age of 20, won the Chess Olympiad — and each of those young grandmasters says the same thing: Rustam showed us it was possible.

Kitob jadvali 4 qator: ANY (istalgan biri) + birlik ot + birlik fe'l; BOTH (ikkalasi) + ko'plik ot + ko'plik fe'l; ALL (hammasi) + ko'plik ot + ko'plik fe'l (all + sanalmas ot — birlik: all water is); NONE (hech biri) + of + ko'plik ot + birlik/ko'plik fe'l. 11-dars bilan solishtirish: neither (2) — none (3+); either (2) — any (3+); both (2) — all (3+).

intro: ANY — istalgan biri (3+): "Any student can answer." (+ birlik ot, birlik fe'l).
BOTH — ikkalasi: "Both players are ready." (+ ko'plik ot, ko'plik fe'l). both of them / both the boys / both … and …
ALL — hammasi (3+): "All students have passed." (+ ko'plik); all + sanalmas: "All information is useful." all of us / all the money.
NONE — hech biri (3+): "None of the books is available." (rasmiy — birlik; og'zaki — are). "none" yolg'iz ham: "None came."
Juftlar: either/any, neither/none, both/all — 2 va 3+.
formulas: Any student can answer the question.
Istalgan talaba bu savolga javob bera oladi.
All + ko'plik ot + ko'plik fe'l / All + sanalmas + birlik
All students have passed the exam. / All poverty is a problem.
Barcha talabalar imtihondan o'tdi. / Har qanday qashshoqlik — muammo.
None of + ko'plik ot + birlik (rasmiy) / ko'plik fe'l
None of the books is available.
both / either / neither (2) — all / any / none (3+)
Both parents work. / All parents work. / Neither parent works. / None of the parents work.
Ikkala ota-ona ishlaydi. / Hamma ota-onalar ishlaydi. / Hech qaysi ota-ona ishlamaydi.
both of / all of / none of / any of + olmosh/the + ot
Both of them agree. / All of the money was donated. / None of us knew.
Ikkalasi ham rozi. / Hamma pul ehson qilindi. / Hech birimiz bilmasdik.

reading.title: Malala Yousafzai — all girls have the right to learn
text: Malala Yousafzai was born in 1997 in the Swat valley in Pakistan. Her father ran a school, and both of her parents believed that all children — boys and girls — should study. But in 2007 the Taliban took control of the valley. They closed all girls' schools; none of the 50,000 girls in Swat could go to class.

Malala was 11. Any girl who spoke out was in danger, yet she started writing a blog for the BBC about life without school. Both her name and her face became known. In October 2012, gunmen stopped her school bus and shot her in the head. Neither the doctors in Pakistan nor the doctors in England were sure she would live. She did.

After her recovery she did not stop. She spoke at the United Nations on her 16th birthday: "One child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world." In 2014 she became the youngest person ever to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Her fund has built schools in Pakistan, Nigeria and Syria, and all of its projects have one goal: 12 years of free education for every girl.

Today Malala has finished Oxford University and is married. She has visited many countries, and both students and presidents listen to her. "I tell my story," she says, "not because it is unique, but because it is not. It is the story of many girls." None of them, she believes, should be silent.

intro: THE NUMBER OF + ko'plik ot + BIRLIK fe'l (son bitta): "The number of students is increasing."
A NUMBER OF + ko'plik ot + KO'PLIK fe'l (= many): "A number of students are late."
NONE / SOME / ALL / MOST OF + ko'plik ot → ko'plik fe'l; + sanalmas ot → birlik: "Some of the water is cold."
EITHER … OR / NEITHER … NOR — fe'l OXIRGI egaga mos: "Either John or his friends are coming." / "Neither the students nor the teacher is here."
GERUND ega → birlik: "Swimming is fun." ONE OF THE + ko'plik → birlik: "One of the students is absent."

reading.title: Abdulla Avloni — "Upbringing is a matter of life or death"
text: Abdulla Avloni was born in 1878 in Tashkent, in a family of craftsmen. Reading was his passion from childhood: one of his teachers said that the number of books the boy read in a year was higher than the whole class read together. At 20 he was already a teacher, and at 26 he opened his own school — a new-method school, where children learned by understanding, not by repeating.

Avloni believed that education is not only knowledge. In 1913 he wrote "Turkiy Guliston yoxud Axloq" (The Turkic Garden, or Ethics), a textbook about character: patience, courage, honesty, gratitude, humility and self-discipline. Its most famous sentence is still quoted in every Uzbek school: "Upbringing is, for us, a matter of life or death, of salvation or destruction." A number of his ideas — daily habits, self-control, learning from mistakes — are exactly what modern books on personal development teach.

He was also a playwright and founded one of the first Uzbek theatres, because he thought that either a lesson or a play could change a person, and a play works faster. He wrote poems, published a newspaper and, after 1917, worked as a diplomat in Afghanistan and as a professor in Tashkent.
Avloni died in 1934. Neither fame nor money was his goal; teaching was. Today one of the largest pedagogical institutes in Tashkent is named after him, and none of his ideas has become old.

intro: -ING CLAUSE — ega o'zi bajaradi, asosiy gap bilan bir vaqtda yoki sabab: "Walking down the street, she saw an old friend." (= While she was walking…) "Feeling tired, I went to bed." (= Because I felt tired…)
-ING EGA SIFATIDA — gerund: "Studying late at night is tiring." (+ birlik fe'l).
-ED CLAUSE — egaga nisbatan bajarilgan (passiv): "Shocked by the news, he couldn't say a word." (= Because he was shocked…) "Built in 2015, the model is old."
Otdan keyin: "The student sitting there is Ali." (= who is sitting) / "The data collected by sensors is huge." (= which was collected).

reading.title: Sam Altman — the man who gave the world ChatGPT
text: Sam Altman was born in 1985 in Chicago. Given his first computer at eight, he taught himself to program. Studying at Stanford, he started a company called Loopt at 19 — and, wanting to build it full-time, he dropped out. Later he ran Y Combinator, the famous startup school that helped companies such as Airbnb and Dropbox.

In 2015 Altman and Elon Musk co-founded OpenAI, a non-profit created to make sure that artificial intelligence would be safe for everyone. Trained on almost the whole internet, OpenAI's language models became better every year. Then, in November 2022, the company released ChatGPT. Used by 100 million people in two months, it became the fastest-growing app in history. Students in Tashkent, doctors in London and farmers in India were all typing prompts into the same chatbot.

In November 2023 something strange happened: Altman was fired by OpenAI's board. Shocked by the decision, almost all 700 employees threatened to leave. Five days later he was back. Asked what he had learned, he said: "Build things people want, and take care of your team."

Altman says AI will change work more than the internet did. Worried about job displacement and deepfakes, he asks governments for regulation — of his own product. Not everyone trusts him; critics say a company growing this fast cannot regulate itself. But nobody argues with one fact: talking to a machine, we no longer feel surprised. That is his doing.

lessons.grammar_topic: ANIQLOVCHI ERGASH GAPLAR — WHO / WHICH / THAT (ega va to'ldiruvchi vazifasida)

objectives: who (odam) / which (narsa) / that (ikkalasi) bilan ikki gapni bitta gapga birlashtirish.
Ega va to'ldiruvchi relative clause farqi; to'ldiruvchi bo'lganda olmoshni tushirish (The phone she bought).
Defining (vergulsiz, muhim ma'lumot) va non-defining (vergulli, qo'shimcha; that ishlatilmaydi).

timeline: Ustoz: "A miner is a person. He checks transactions." → "A miner is a person who checks transactions." "Bitcoin is a currency. It has no bank." → "Bitcoin is a currency which has no bank." O'quvchilar: odam → who, narsa → which.
20 savol, 15 soniya; oldingi dars lug'ati + grammatikasi.
YOZMA NORMATIV — Progress test 3 natijalari + -ing/-ed clauses lug'ati

Kitob jadvali 4 qator: WHO ega (who + fe'l), WHO(M) to'ldiruvchi (who + ega + fe'l — tushirib qoldirsa bo'ladi), WHICH/THAT ega (which + fe'l), WHICH/THAT to'ldiruvchi (which + ega + fe'l — tushirsa bo'ladi). that — og'zaki, ikkalasi uchun. Defining (vergulsiz) vs non-defining (vergulli, that yo'q).
Har so'z bilan yangi grammatika qolipida gap.
Kitob: formula → gap → tarjima; warm-up / normativ / coin me'yorlari.
Sinf matni + 3 topshiriq; kitob Topic'lari uyga.
Yangi grammatika bilan 5 gap (yozma) yoki 1 daqiqa og'zaki.
Ko'p uchragan xatolar doskada; STRONG lug'at kuchlilarga.

intro: WHO — odam: "The girl who called you is my cousin." (who = ega: who + fe'l).
WHO(M) — odam, to'ldiruvchi: "The boy (who) you met is my friend." (who + ega + fe'l → tushirsa bo'ladi; whom — rasmiy).
WHICH / THAT — narsa: "The car which broke down was expensive." (ega) / "The phone (which) she bought is new." (to'ldiruvchi, tushirsa bo'ladi).
Non-defining: qo'shimcha ma'lumot, vergul bilan, that EMAS: "Bitcoin, which was created in 2009, has no bank."
Ikki ega xatosi: "The phone which she bought it" — "it" ortiqcha.

reading.title: Satoshi Nakamoto — the person who invented Bitcoin and disappeared
text: On 31 October 2008, someone who called himself Satoshi Nakamoto posted a nine-page document on a small internet forum. It was a whitepaper which described a new kind of money: a currency that no bank, no government and no company would control. Three months later the first Bitcoin block, which is now called the "genesis block", was created. Inside it Satoshi wrote a newspaper headline about banks that were being rescued by the government — a message that many people read as a joke and a warning.

For two years Satoshi worked with the programmers who joined the project. He wrote thousands of messages, but he never gave an interview, never showed his face and never told anyone where he lived. Then, in April 2011, he sent his last email: "I've moved on to other things." He has not been heard from since.

Who is he? Nobody knows. Some think he is a British cryptographer whose writing style matches; others think Satoshi is a group. A man who was named by a magazine in 2014 denied everything. The wallet which belongs to Satoshi holds about one million bitcoins — worth tens of billions of dollars — and not one coin has ever been moved.

Today Bitcoin is a currency (that) 500 million people own, and the blockchain which Satoshi designed is used by banks he wanted to replace. The person who started it all wanted only one thing: a system that works without trust in any single person — including himself.

intro: WHERE — joy haqida qo'shimcha ma'lumot, ish o'sha joyda bo'ladi: "The city where I was born is beautiful." / "This is the café where we met." (where + ega + fe'l).
WHICH — joy gapning egasi/to'ldiruvchisi: "This is the house which was built in 1920." (which + fe'l) / "The shop which I like is closed." (which + ega + fe'l, predlogsiz).
IN/AT/ON WHICH — where'ning rasmiy shakli: "This is the school in which I studied." = "the school where I studied" = "the school (which) I studied at".
Test: gapni to'liq qaytar — "I studied IN the school" → in bor → where / in which; "The school was built" → predlog yo'q → which.

reading.title: Jack Ma — the teacher who built the biggest online market in the world
text: Jack Ma was born in 1964 in Hangzhou, a city where tourists came to see the West Lake. As a boy he waited near the hotel where foreigners stayed and offered them free tours in exchange for English practice. He failed the university entrance exam twice. Later he applied for 30 jobs, including KFC, where 24 people were accepted and he was the only one rejected. So he became an English teacher, earning 12 dollars a month.

In 1995 he visited the USA, where he saw the internet for the first time. He typed "beer" and found results from many countries, but none from China. Back home, in 1999, he gathered 17 friends in his flat — the flat which is now a museum — and founded Alibaba, a marketplace where small Chinese factories could sell to the world.

Alibaba grew into a company which handles more sales than Amazon and eBay together. Taobao, the site where ordinary people sell to each other, has 900 million users. On Singles' Day, the shopping festival which Alibaba invented, the platform sells more in one day than most countries do in a year.

Ma retired in 2019 to return to education. "I'm a teacher," he says. "Alibaba was just a lesson." The lesson which he repeats most: "Today is hard, tomorrow is harder, but the day after tomorrow is beautiful — most people give up tomorrow night."

intro: WHOSE — egalik ("…ning"): "The man whose car was stolen called the police." whose + ot (whose car). Narsalar uchun ham: "a country whose energy is green".
WHY — sabab: "That is the reason why I left early." (why tushirsa bo'ladi: the reason I left).
WHEN — vaqt: "I remember the day when we first met." (when tushirsa/that bilan almashtirsa bo'ladi).
Xarita: odam → who; narsa → which/that; joy → where; egalik → whose; sabab → why; vaqt → when.
formulas: The man whose car was stolen called the police.
Mashinasi o'g'irlangan odam politsiyaga qo'ng'iroq qildi.
A country whose energy is renewable pollutes less.
Energiyasi qayta tiklanuvchi mamlakat kamroq ifloslaydi.
That is the reason why I left early.
I remember the day when we first met.
the reason (why) / the day (when) / the year (that)

reading.title: Nikola Tesla — the inventor whose ideas were a century early
text: Nikola Tesla was born in 1856 in a small village in today's Croatia, in a family whose father was a priest. As a student he could see machines in his head and test them without building them. In 1884 he arrived in New York with four cents in his pocket and a letter for Thomas Edison, whose company used direct current (DC). Tesla believed in alternating current (AC), a system whose electricity could travel hundreds of kilometres. The two men argued, and Tesla left.

1888 was the year when he sold his AC patents to George Westinghouse, and 1893 was the year when AC lit the Chicago World's Fair. Soon after, Tesla's system was used to send electricity from Niagara Falls to the city of Buffalo — the moment when the modern grid was born. Today almost every wire in the world carries the current whose design he made.

Tesla had hundreds of ideas: the electric motor, radio, remote control, neon lights and wireless electricity. In his laboratory he produced lightning indoors. But he was a scientist whose interest was ideas, not money. He tore up a contract that would have made him a billionaire, because he didn't want Westinghouse to go bankrupt. That is the reason why he died in 1943 in a hotel room, alone and poor.

His name is now on the unit of magnetic field and on the electric-car company whose founder calls him the greatest engineer ever. Renewable energy — solar, wind, hydro — all of it travels on Tesla's system.

intro: Ega ergash gap = butun gap egа o'rnida: "[What he said] is true." Fe'l — BIRLIK (is).
WHAT — nima ekanligi: "What matters is time." HOW — qanday qilib: "How he solved it is amazing."
WHETHER — ikki imkoniyat: "Whether she comes is unknown." (if — ega bo'la olmaydi!). THAT — fakt: "That she passed the exam is surprising." (= It is surprising that she passed.)
WHOEVER / WHATEVER — kim/nima bo'lsa ham: "Whoever arrives first will get a prize." / "Whatever happens is your responsibility."
Ega ergash gap ichida so'z tartibi — gapdek (ega + fe'l), savol tartibi emas: "What he does" (what does he — xato).

reading.title: Warren Buffett — what he does with money is simple
text: Warren Buffett was born in 1930 in Omaha, a small city in the middle of the USA. What he loved as a boy was numbers. At six he sold chewing gum door to door; at eleven he bought his first shares; at fourteen he had a newspaper round that earned more than his teachers. That a teenager could save 5,000 dollars in the 1940s was unusual — but Buffett was unusual.

How he became the most famous investor in history is surprisingly simple. He buys companies that he understands, that have honest managers and that will still exist in thirty years — and then he waits. Whether the market goes up or down next month does not interest him. "Our favourite holding period," he says, "is forever." What made him rich was not clever trading but compound interest and patience: 99% of his wealth came after his 50th birthday.

Whoever meets Buffett is shocked by how he lives. He still lives in the house he bought in 1958 for 31,500 dollars. He drives an old car, drinks five cans of cola a day and eats at McDonald's. What he spends on himself is tiny. What he gives away is enormous: he has pledged 99% of his fortune — more than 100 billion dollars — to charity.

Every year he writes a letter to his shareholders, and millions of ordinary people read it like a textbook. His rule for beginners is the shortest in finance: "Rule number one: never lose money. Rule number two: never forget rule number one." Whatever you earn, he adds, spend less than that — and start early.

Kitob jadvali 7 qator: THAT (aniq fikr: She said that she was tired), WH-so'zlar (I don't know where she lives), WHETHER / IF (…mi-yo'qmi: I don't know if she will come), WHOEVER (invite whoever you like), WHATEVER (do whatever you want), HOW (I can't explain how it works), WHY (I don't understand why she left). intro: THAT — fikr/fakt: "She said that she was tired." (that tushirsa bo'ladi: She said she was tired.)
WH-so'zlar — what/where/when/who/why/how: "I don't know where she lives." (where + ega + fe'l — savol tartibi EMAS).
WHETHER / IF — ikki imkoniyat: "I don't know if/whether she will come." (to'ldiruvchi bo'lganda if ham bo'ladi).
WHOEVER / WHATEVER: "You can invite whoever you like." / "You can do whatever you want."
Ega (18) vs to'ldiruvchi (19): "What she said is true" (ega) — "I know what she said" (to'ldiruvchi).
formulas: She said that she was tired.

I can't explain how it works.
I don't understand why she left.

ask/wonder/know + if/whether; "I wonder if…" — muloyim savol.

reading.title: Greta Thunberg — the girl who told the world what science says
text: Greta Thunberg was born in 2003 in Stockholm. When she was eight, a teacher showed the class what climate change was doing to the planet. Other children forgot it by lunchtime; Greta could not. She read everything she could find and understood that scientists had been saying the same thing for thirty years — and that almost nobody was listening.

In August 2018, at fifteen, she decided that she would not go to school on Fridays. Instead she sat in front of the Swedish parliament with a sign: "School strike for the climate." She said that there was no point in studying for a future that adults were destroying. At first she sat alone. Within a year, millions of students in 150 countries were striking with her.

In 2019 she was invited to the United Nations in New York. Because she believes that flying produces too much carbon, she sailed across the Atlantic in a small boat for two weeks. At the UN she told the leaders that they had stolen her childhood with their empty words: "How dare you!" The speech was watched hundreds of millions of times. Time magazine named her Person of the Year — the youngest ever.

Greta says that she is not a scientist and that people should not listen to her, but to the science. Whether her strikes changed politics is still debated. What nobody doubts is that a teenager made the whole world talk about how fast the ice is melting.

intro: SIMPLE ACTIVE — V-ing: "I like reading books." Ega bajaradi.
SIMPLE PASSIVE — being + V3: "He dislikes being told what to do." Egaga nisbatan bajariladi.
PERFECT ACTIVE — having + V3: "He regrets having wasted time." (oldin bo'lgan ish).
PERFECT PASSIVE — having been + V3: "She remembers having been given an award."

Gerund keladi: enjoy/avoid/mind/suggest/finish/keep/practise/consider/deny/admit/miss/risk + V-ing; predlogdan keyin (interested in protecting, without asking, after leaving); ega/to'ldiruvchi sifatida.
formulas: He dislikes being told what to do.
U nima qilish kerakligini aytishlarini yoqtirmaydi.
She remembers having been given an award.
enjoy / avoid / mind / suggest / finish / keep + V-ing
Qo'riqchilar bog'ni patrul qilishda davom etadi.
in / at / of / without / after / before + V-ing

Ba'zi fe'llar gerund va infinitiv bilan ma'no o'zgartiradi (21-dars): stop/remember/forget/try/regret.

reading.title: David Attenborough — seventy years of filming the wild
text: David Attenborough was born in 1926 in London. As a boy he enjoyed collecting fossils and birds' eggs, and he dreamed of seeing every animal in the world. After studying natural sciences at Cambridge, he joined the BBC in 1952. Being sent to Africa to film animals for television was, he says, the luckiest thing that ever happened to him.

Since then he has spent seventy years narrating nature documentaries — "Life on Earth", "Planet Earth", "Blue Planet" — watched by billions of people. Filming a snow leopard hunting took his team three years of waiting in the Himalayas. He admits having been afraid many times: of gorillas, of snakes, of falling off cliffs. But he never regrets having gone.

In the last twenty years his message has changed. Instead of only showing beauty, he keeps warning: half of the world's wildlife has disappeared since he started filming. "Saving the planet," he says, "is now a communications challenge." His 2017 film about plastic in the ocean led to millions of people giving up plastic bags — and to new laws in Britain.

At 99 he is still working. He regrets having flown so much, and he now records most of his narration at home. Asked what young people should do, he answers with one word: "Care." Caring about nature, he says, is the first step; protecting it comes next.

lessons.grammar_topic: INFINITIV — to V1 / to be V3 / to be V-ing / to have V3 / to have been V3
lessons.book_ref: Student's book IELTS 3.0: Lesson 21 – Infinitive (6 qatorli jadval); SPACE EXPLORATION (70 so'z); Reading — Vladimir Dzhanibekov (Jony Academy matni); kitob Topic 146–150 uyga.
objectives: Infinitivning 6 shaklini tanish va tuzish; perfect infinitiv — oldin bo'lgan ish (claims to have seen).
Infinitiv talab qiladigan fe'llar (want, decide, hope, seem, claim, manage, refuse…).
Gerund/infinitiv ma'no farqi: stop to do / stop doing; remember to do / remember doing; try to / try -ing.
Koinot CORE 20 bilan kosmos va O'zbekiston kosmonavti haqida gapirish.
timeline: Ustoz: "She wants to fly. The rocket needs to be checked. He seems to be sleeping. He claims to have seen a UFO. She is happy to have been chosen." — 6 infinitiv shakli doskada; o'quvchilar faol/passiv, oddiy/davomli/perfect deb belgilaydi.
20 savol, 15 soniya; oldingi dars lug'ati + grammatikasi.

Kitob jadvali 6 qator: Simple Active (to V1), Simple Passive (to be + V3), Continuous Active (to be + V-ing), Continuous Passive (to be being + V3 — kam), Perfect Active (to have + V3), Perfect Passive (to have been + V3). Infinitiv talab qiladigan fe'llar: want, need, decide, hope, plan, promise, refuse, seem, claim, manage, afford, agree, offer. Gerund vs infinitiv ma'no farqi: stop/remember/forget/try/regret.
Har so'z bilan yangi grammatika qolipida gap.
Kitob: formula → gap → tarjima; warm-up / normativ / coin me'yorlari.
Sinf matni + 3 topshiriq; kitob Topic'lari uyga.
Yangi grammatika bilan 5 gap (yozma) yoki 1 daqiqa og'zaki.
Ko'p uchragan xatolar doskada; STRONG lug'at kuchlilarga.

intro: SIMPLE ACTIVE — to + V1: "She wants to learn English."
SIMPLE PASSIVE — to be + V3: "The book needs to be read."
CONTINUOUS ACTIVE — to be + V-ing: "She seems to be sleeping." (Continuous passive — to be being + V3 — juda kam).
PERFECT ACTIVE — to have + V3: "He claims to have seen a ghost." (oldin bo'lgan). PERFECT PASSIVE — to have been + V3: "She is happy to have been given the award."
Farq: stop to rest (dam olish uchun to'xtadi) / stop resting (dam olishni to'xtatdi); remember to call (qo'ng'iroq qilishni unutma) / remember calling (qo'ng'iroq qilganini eslaydi).

reading.title: Vladimir Dzhanibekov — the Tashkent cosmonaut who saved a dead station
text: Vladimir Dzhanibekov was born in 1942 in a village near Tashkent, in the Bostanlyk district. As a boy he wanted to be a physicist, but after seeing the first cosmonauts he decided to become a pilot. In 1970 he was chosen to be trained as a cosmonaut. He is known to have flown into space five times — a record at the time — and to have been named Hero of the Soviet Union twice.

His most famous flight was in 1985. The Salyut-7 space station had stopped answering: its batteries had died, and it was flying uncontrolled, frozen and dark. Nobody had ever tried to dock with a dead station by hand. Dzhanibekov and his partner Viktor Savinykh were asked to do it. They managed to approach the station, to dock manually and to open the door. Inside it was −10 degrees; water had frozen on the walls. Working in winter clothes and hats, they managed to repair the electrical system over eight days. Engineers later called it the most difficult repair in the history of spaceflight.

On the same flight he noticed something strange: a wing nut spinning in zero gravity seemed to flip over by itself every few seconds. Physicists now call it the Dzhanibekov effect, and it is used to explain how planets and satellites rotate.

He retired from flying in 1985 and later worked as a general, an artist and a professor. Today a street in Tashkent and a school in his home district are named after him, and every Uzbek child who hopes to fly to space is told his story first.

lessons.title: Gerund / Infinitive as Subject
lessons.grammar_topic: GERUND va INFINITIV EGA VAZIFASIDA (Swimming is good / To swim is fun) + gerund/infinitiv tanlash
lessons.book_ref: Student's book IELTS 3.0: Lesson 22 – Gerund/infinitive as subject (2 qatorli jadval); GLOBAL ECONOMY (61 so'z); Reading — Jeff Bezos (Jony Academy matni); kitob Topic 151–155 uyga; Writing 10: Living with parents vs. living alone.
objectives: Gerund va infinitivni ega sifatida ishlatish; fe'l — birlik.
"To V1 is …" → "It is … to V1" almashinuvi (tabiiy uslub).
Gerund/infinitiv fe'llar xaritasi: faqat gerund / faqat infinitiv / ikkalasi / ma'no farqi.
Jahon iqtisodiyoti CORE 20 bilan savdo, import-eksport va globallashuv haqida gapirish; Writing 10.
timeline: Ustoz: "Trading is old. To trade is human." — ikkalasi ega; o'quvchilar: qaysi biri tabiiyroq (gerund), qaysi biri rasmiy/she'riy (infinitiv)? "It is important to trade" — uchinchi yo'l.
20 savol, 15 soniya; oldingi dars lug'ati + grammatikasi.

Kitob jadvali: Gerund as subject (V-ing + birlik fe'l: Swimming is good for health); Infinitive as subject (To + V1 + birlik fe'l: To swim is fun — rasmiy; odatda "It is fun to swim"). Qo'shimcha: 20–21-dars xulosasi — gerund fe'llari (enjoy, avoid, mind, suggest, finish, keep, consider) vs infinitiv fe'llari (want, decide, hope, plan, refuse, manage, afford) vs ikkalasi (like, love, start, begin, continue, prefer) vs ma'no farqi (stop, remember, forget, try, regret).
Har so'z bilan yangi grammatika qolipida gap.
Kitob: formula → gap → tarjima; warm-up / normativ / coin me'yorlari.
Sinf matni + 3 topshiriq; kitob Topic'lari uyga.
Yangi grammatika bilan 5 gap (yozma) yoki 1 daqiqa og'zaki.
Ko'p uchragan xatolar doskada; STRONG lug'at kuchlilarga.

intro: GERUND EGA — tabiiy, umumiy: "Swimming is good for health." "Exporting cotton was Uzbekistan's main income."
INFINITIV EGA — rasmiy/she'riy: "To swim is fun." Odatda "It is fun to swim." / "It is hard to compete with China."
Fe'l birlik: "Trading is…", "To trade is…" (are — xato).

Xarita: enjoy/avoid/mind/suggest/finish/keep/consider/deny + V-ing; want/decide/hope/plan/refuse/manage/afford/agree + to V1; like/love/hate/start/begin/continue/prefer + ikkalasi; stop/remember/forget/try/regret — ma'no farqi.
formulas: It is hard to compete with China.
enjoy / avoid / mind / suggest / finish / keep / consider + V-ing
Countries avoid raising tariffs in a crisis.
want / decide / hope / plan / refuse / manage / afford + to V1
The company decided to expand abroad.
Kompaniya chet elga kengayishga qaror qildi.
stop / remember / forget / try / regret + V-ing / to V1
They stopped trading with Russia. / They stopped to trade at the border.
Ular Rossiya bilan savdoni to'xtatdi. / Ular chegarada savdo qilish uchun to'xtadi.
presentation: Is exporting cotton still important for Uzbekistan?
Exporting cotton is less important now; exporting gold is bigger.
Is it easy to start a business here?

Do you remember paying customs at the border?

What did Bezos decide to do in 1994?

Why is it hard to compete with China?

notes: Gerund ega — og'zaki va yozma; "To V1" ega — faqat rasmiy/she'riy; imtihonda "It is … to V1" xavfsiz.
Ega gerund uzun bo'lsa ham fe'l birlik: "Selling goods to 200 countries is Amazon's business."
like + to V1 (odat/tanlov) vs like + V-ing (zavq): "I like to check prices" / "I like shopping".

reading.title: Jeff Bezos — selling everything to everyone
text: Jeff Bezos was born in 1964 in New Mexico. Working on his grandfather's ranch in summer taught him to repair anything with his hands. Studying computer science at Princeton taught him something else: that the internet was growing 2,300% a year. In 1994 he had a good job at a bank in New York. Leaving it to sell books online seemed crazy to everyone — except his parents, who gave him 250,000 dollars.

Choosing the name Amazon was deliberate: he wanted the biggest river for the biggest shop. Starting in a garage in Seattle, the company sold its first book in 1995. To make a profit was not the goal; to grow was. For years Amazon lost money, and investors kept asking when it would stop. Bezos refused to change: "It is better to think in decades than in quarters."

His strategy was simple. Keeping prices low brought customers; having more customers attracted more sellers; having more sellers lowered prices again. Building warehouses near every big city made next-day delivery possible. Then, in 2006, Amazon started renting its computers to other companies — cloud services — and that business now earns more than the shop.

Bezos stepped down as CEO in 2021 and now spends his money on rockets: his company Blue Origin plans to build hotels in orbit. Critics say that paying warehouse workers more would be a better idea. Bezos answers with his favourite rule: "It is always Day One." Being finished, he says, is the beginning of the end.

lessons.grammar_topic: KAUZATIV — HAVE / GET + OB'EKT + V3 (boshqa birovga qildirmoq), barcha zamonlarda
lessons.book_ref: Student's book IELTS 3.0: Lesson 23 – Causative voice (have smth done) (7 qatorli jadval); ORGANIC FARMING (65 so'z); Reading — King Charles III's organic farm (Jony Academy matni); kitob Topic 156–160 uyga.
objectives: have + ob'ekt + V3 qolipini 7 zamonda tuzish (zamon "have" da o'zgaradi, V3 doim).
get something done (og'zaki) va have someone do / get someone to do farqi.
Kauzativ vs passiv: "I had the roof repaired" (buyurdim) vs "The roof was repaired" (kim — muhim emas).
Organik dehqonchilik CORE 20 bilan tuproq, o'g'it va hosil haqida gapirish.
timeline: Ustoz: "I cut my hair." (o'zim) — "I have my hair cut." (sartarosh). "The farmer fixed the tractor" — "The farmer had the tractor fixed." — kim qildi? O'quvchilar: kauzativ = boshqa odam qiladi, men buyuraman/to'layman.
20 savol, 15 soniya; oldingi dars lug'ati + grammatikasi.
YOZMA NORMATIV — Gerund / infinitive as subject lug'ati

Kitob jadvali 7 qator: have + ob'ekt + V3 barcha zamonlarda — Present Simple (have my room cleaned), Past (had my computer fixed), Future (will have the report written), Present Continuous (is having the car repaired), Past Continuous (were having the house painted), Present Perfect (have had the emails sent), Past Perfect (had had the roof repaired by 2020). get + ob'ekt + V3 — og'zaki; have + odam + V1 (have the mechanic fix it); get + odam + to V1.
Har so'z bilan yangi grammatika qolipida gap.
Kitob: formula → gap → tarjima; warm-up / normativ / coin me'yorlari.
Sinf matni + 3 topshiriq; kitob Topic'lari uyga.
Yangi grammatika bilan 5 gap (yozma) yoki 1 daqiqa og'zaki.
Ko'p uchragan xatolar doskada; STRONG lug'at kuchlilarga.

intro: KAUZATIV — ish boshqa odam tomonidan mening buyrug'im/to'lovim bilan qilinadi: "I have my room cleaned" (kimdir tozalaydi).
Qolip: HAVE (zamonda) + OB'EKT + V3. Zamon have da: had / will have / is having / has had / had had…
GET + ob'ekt + V3 — og'zaki: "I got the tractor fixed."
Odam ko'rsatilsa: have + somebody + V1 ("I had the mechanic fix it") / get + somebody + to V1 ("I got my brother to help").
Salbiy tajriba ham: "He had his phone stolen" (telefonini o'g'irlatdi).
formulas: Every day I have my room cleaned.
She will have the report written.
She is having the car repaired. / We were having the house painted.
U mashinasini ta'mirlatyapti. / Biz uyni bo'yatayotgan edik.
S + have/has had (had had) + ob'ekt + V3
I have had the emails sent. / He had had the roof repaired by 2020.
Men emaillarni jo'nattirdim. / U 2020-gacha tomni ta'mirlatgan edi.
get + ob'ekt + V3; have + odam + V1; get + odam + to V1
I got the soil tested. / I had the farmer plant trees. / I got him to help.
Tuproqni tekshirtirdim. / Fermerga daraxt ektirdim. / Uni yordam berishga ko'ndirdim.
presentation: Do you have your soil tested every year?

Yes, he had it repaired last week.

No, we won't have it sprayed — it's organic.

notes: V3 doim: "have it repaired" (repair, repairing — xato).
Zamon faqat "have" da: has had / had had (ikki had — to'g'ri!).
Kauzativ savol: "Did you have it fixed?" / "Are you having it built?"
Organic lug'ati: soil, fertile, compost, manure, pesticide, crop rotation, free-range, certification, farm-to-table.
mistakes: I had repaired my car. (boshqa odam)

reading.title: King Charles III — the prince who had his farm made organic
text: Charles was born in 1948 and waited 73 years to become king — longer than anyone in British history. While he was waiting, he had a lot of time for his real passion: farming. In 1980 he bought Highgrove, an old house with 300 hectares of land in the west of England, and in 1985 he made a decision that farmers laughed at: he had the whole estate converted to organic farming.

At that time almost nobody farmed without chemicals. Charles had the pesticides stopped, had crop rotation introduced and had kilometres of hedgerows planted for birds and insects. He had rare breeds of sheep and cattle brought back and had beehives placed in the orchards. Journalists mocked him for saying that he talked to his plants. By 1986 he had had the farm certified organic — one of the first in the country.

In 1990 he had a brand created, Duchy Originals, and had its biscuits made with organic oats from his own fields. Every pound of profit was given to charity — more than 30 million pounds so far. Supermarkets that had refused organic food in the 1980s now have entire shelves filled with it.

Today the king still gardens himself at Highgrove, though he has the heavy work done by others. "People said I was ahead of my time," he says. "I was just listening to the soil." Since he became king in 2022, he has had organic methods introduced on royal farms across the country.

reading.title: Abdulla Qodiriy — could you tell me who wrote the first Uzbek novel?
text: If you ask any Uzbek student who wrote the first Uzbek novel, they will tell you at once: Abdulla Qodiriy. He was born in 1894 in Tashkent, in a poor family; his father was a gardener. Do you know how he learned to write? At a Russian-native school, then in a madrasa, and finally by himself, reading Russian and Tatar newspapers. At 20 he was already publishing stories under the pen name Julqunboy.

In 1922 he began "O'tkan kunlar" (Bygone Days), and in 1926 it came out as a book. Could you tell me why it was so important? Because Uzbek literature had poetry, tales and epics, but no novel — no long story with real characters, a plot and a setting in a real city. The love of Otabek and Kumush, set in Tashkent and Margilan in the 1840s, became the book that everyone read. His second novel, "Mehrobdan chayon" (Scorpion from the Altar), followed in 1929.

Qodiriy was also a satirist: he wrote humorous articles about corruption and stupidity, and that made him enemies. In 1926 he was arrested for the first time; in 1937, during the great repression, he was arrested again. Nobody knows exactly where he was buried after he was shot in October 1938. His books were banned for twenty years.

He was rehabilitated in 1956, and today "O'tkan kunlar" is read in every school, has been adapted into films and has been translated into English. Would you mind reading it before you finish IELTS 3.0? Many students say it is the best way to fall in love with your own language.

PARTICIPLE 2 — V3, PASSIV, otga nisbatan bajarilgan: "the broken window" (oyna sindirilgan), "the house built in 1990" (uy qurilgan).
Otdan keyingi participle = relative clause qisqasi: "the film (which was) directed by Nolan" → "the film directed by Nolan".
Sifat sifatida his-tuyg'u: boring (film) / bored (tomoshabin) — 2.0 24-dars.
Qo'shimcha: having + V3 (oldin tugagan): "Having finished the film, we left." being + V3: "The film being shown now is new."

reading.title: Christopher Nolan — the director making films inside dreams
text: Christopher Nolan was born in London in 1970. A boy given a camera at seven, he spent his childhood making short films with toy soldiers. Studying literature at university, he ran the film society and made his first feature film, "Following", on weekends — a black-and-white thriller shot for 6,000 dollars with actors working for free.

His second film, "Memento" (2000), made him famous. It is a detective story told backwards: the viewer, knowing only what the hero remembers, is as confused as he is. Critics writing about it used one word — genius. Then came the Batman trilogy, released between 2005 and 2012, with the Joker played by Heath Ledger, an actor given an Oscar after his death.

"Inception" (2010) is a heist film set inside dreams, with a corridor rotating 360 degrees built for real and a spinning top at the end never explained. "Interstellar" (2014) is science fiction based on real physics, with a black hole designed by a Nobel-winning physicist. Nolan hates CGI: the plane crash shown in "Tenet" was filmed with a real plane, and the explosion opening "Oppenheimer" was made without computers.

"Oppenheimer" (2023), a biopic telling the story of the man building the atomic bomb, earned almost a billion dollars and won seven Oscars, including Best Director — Nolan's first. He still writes every screenplay by hand, uses no email and does not allow phones on set. Audiences leaving his films usually say the same thing: "I need to watch that again."

intro: FUTURE IN THE PAST — o'tgan nuqtadan qaralganda kelajak: "In 2022 he said he would call" (o'shanda kelajak edi).
4 shakl: would + V1; would be + V-ing; would have + V3; would have been + V-ing — Future Simple/Continuous/Perfect/Perfect Continuous'ning "o'tgan" versiyasi.
Qo'llanish: reported speech (said/thought/knew/promised + would), hikoya ("She didn't know that she would become champion"), was/were going to (reja).

Kurs xaritasi: 1 zamonlar → 2–5 used to/tags/pronouns/modal+V3 → 6–9 ravishlar va taqqoslash → 10 shart → 11–13 taqsimlovchi/moslik → 14, 25 sifatdosh → 15–19 ergash gaplar → 20–22 gerund/infinitiv → 23 kauzativ → 24 bilvosita savol → 26 future in the past.

reading.title: Uzbekistan's road to the World Cup — they said they would, and they did
text: In 1994 Uzbekistan played its first international match as an independent country. The players said that one day the team would play at a World Cup. For thirty years it seemed that day would never come: in 2014 and 2018 the team lost in the final play-offs, and fans joked that Uzbekistan would always be "the best team that never qualifies".

In 2022 a new coach, Timur Kapadze, took over a young squad. Most of them were teenagers when they said they would change history: Abdukodir Khusanov, who would become the first Uzbek in the Premier League; Eldor Shomurodov, who had been playing in Italy for years; goalkeeper Utkir Yusupov; and a generation that had won the Asian U-20 championship in 2023. Kapadze promised that by June 2025 they would have qualified — and that they would be playing without fear.

On 5 June 2025, in Abu Dhabi, Uzbekistan drew 0–0 with the UAE, and the promise came true: for the first time in history, Uzbekistan would be going to the World Cup. In Tashkent people were dancing in the streets at midnight; the players said they would remember that night for the rest of their lives.

In June 2026 the team will play in North America. Nobody knows how far they will go. But every child in Uzbekistan now knows one thing that the 1994 players only hoped: it would happen — and it did. As the captain said at the airport: "We said we would. Now we will show that we can."
glossary: rest of one's life — umrining oxirigacha
